newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Rome says budget best path for EMU entry.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Rome says budget best path for EMU entry.

text.p: The Italian government on Thursday said its controversial 1997 budget was the best way for the country to participate in Europe's planned single currency but opposition parties vowed to wage a tough battle.

Treasury minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told parliament in a speech opening a debate on the budget that the government's intent to slash the public deficit showed Rome's clear will to be a full participant in EMU.

With the budget, Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government aims to slash next year's public deficit by 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion). The budget is a mix of greater revenues and spending cuts.

Ciampi said official downwards revision of the deficit-GDP ratio for 1997 to three percent as a result of the measures was a signal "to everyone, without a shadow of a doubt, that Italy intends to be in a united Europe, a full-fledged member of that union which our country has actively promoted since its conception".

Ciampi told the lower house of parliament inflation was continuing to fall, leading to lower market interest rates, and that consumer price inflation should be below three precent by the end of the year.
A fall in real interest rates would boost the Italian economy, stimulating investment and jobs and reducing the interest burden on the public debt to manageable levels.
"We have a duty to create credibility. That is the way to reduce interest rates and thus the public deficit," he said.
But the centre-right Freedom Alliance has blasted the budget as an "all-tax" package that will cause recession and not be enough get Italy into monetary union from its 1999 start.
Several hours before Ciampi spoke, former Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi unveiled the centre-right's "counter-budget" proposal, vowing to lead strong opposition.

"With this budget (the government's) we have to have a tough opposition...ours will be strong, true, decisive, determined and certainly never forget the interests of the country," Berlusconi told a news conference.

Among measures included in the goverment's budget is a five percent increase in taxes on house and land ownership as well as a five percent increase in the valuations local authorities can base their property taxes on.

Berlusconi, who served as prime minister for seven months in 1994, criticised a proposal in Prodi's budget for a one-off "Euro-tax" to help Italy achieve the three percent deficit-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio required by the Maastricht treaty to qualify for Economic and Monetary Union.
He said the "Euro-tax" would create "a vicious cycle of economic depression".
Parties backing Prodi also have asked him to remove the unpopular property tax hike from the budget.

"There's no doubt that one of the points that needs to be changed is the (house) tax," Massimo D'Alema, leader of the largest coalition party, the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), told reporters. ($1=1520 Lire)
